screens.title: Updating Documents: Modifiers & Operators
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson will give you a clear, practical view of how MongoDB lets you change data. You will learn the difference between replacing an entire document and updating only specific fields, and why partial updates are usually safer and faster. We'll introduce updateOne and updateMany for targeted changes, explain important field operators like $set, $inc, $unset, and $rename, and then step through array-focused operators such as $push, $addToSet, $pop, and $pull for adding, deduplicating, and removing elements. You will also see the upsert option, which can create-or-update a document in a single call, and we will highlight common mistakes like accidentally running updateMany with an empty filter. Throughout the lesson, we frame each operator with short code examples and before/after states so you can see the transformation. By the end you will know when to use replaceOne versus updateOne, how to manipulate numeric and array fields atomically, and how to design safe updates that minimize data loss and performance issues. Ready to explore the operators and practice a bookstore inventory scenario to make this concrete?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will build four practical skills that make document updates reliable and efficient. First, you will clearly understand the difference between replacing a whole document and updating individual fields, and why partial updates often prevent accidental data loss. For example, replacing a document will remove fields you did not include, which can be surprising if you expect a small change. Second, you will learn to use updateOne and updateMany correctly, choosing the right method when you need to change a single record versus many records at once and avoiding broad filters that update the entire collection. Third, you will practice field operators such as $set and $inc to change or increment values atomically, and $unset or $rename to remove or rename fields. These operators let you evolve documents without replacing them. Fourth, you will master array update operators—$push, $addToSet, $pop, and $pull—to add, deduplicate, and remove array elements safely. Each objective will include a short example and a verification step so you can check results in mongosh.

You will be able to perform create-or-update flows using the upsert option, which inserts when no match exists and updates when one does. Another objective is to verify updates using queries and the. pretty() output so you can confirm before moving on. Finally, you will learn to reason about atomicity: updates are atomic at the document level in MongoDB, so single-document operators like $inc are safe for concurrent increments, but multi-document consistency requires transactions. screens.title: replaceOne() versus updateOne()
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare replacing a document with replaceOne and applying targeted changes with updateOne. replaceOne takes a matching filter and substitutes a new document for the matched one. That means every field not present in the replacement will be removed, except for _id which is preserved. This makes replaceOne appropriate when you intentionally want a complete structural change or to reset a document. In contrast, updateOne with operators modifies only specified fields; it leaves all other fields untouched. A typical pattern uses $set with updateOne to change some fields safely. For example, if a product document has fields stock, tags, and details, replacing it without including tags will remove that information. A common misconception is to assume replaceOne behaves like a partial update; it does not. Always inspect the replacement body. In practice, prefer updateOne with $set for incremental changes, and reserve replaceOne for structural rewrites or migrations. To check your work, run a find query before and after and compare fields. Which approach fits your maintenance policy and rollback plan? replaceOne() versus updateOne() means use replaceone only when you intend a full overwrite; use updateone with $set to change fields without losing other data.. In practical terms, when overwriting a document deletes fields versus when to update only what you need. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › replaceOne vs updateOne
Definition

replaceOne()

Completely replaces the matched document with the provided document. _id is retained; all other fields not included are removed.

Before
{ _id: 1, title: "Old", price: 20, tags: ["sale"], stock: 5 }
Replacement
{ _id: 1, title: "New", price: 30 }
Result: tags and stock are removed because they were not included in the replacement.
Definition

updateOne() with $set

Updates only specified fields and preserves unspecified fields. Use $set to modify or add fields without overwriting the whole document.

Before
{ _id: 1, title: "Old", price: 20, tags: ["sale"], stock: 5 }
Update
{ $set: { price: 30, title: "New" } }
Result: tags and stock remain unchanged.
Common mistake
Using replaceOne when intending partial changes can delete fields unintentionally.
Pro tip
Prefer updateOne with $set for incremental updates and reserve replaceOne for migrations.
Key Takeaway
Replace overwrites; update operators change only what you specify.

screens.title: updateOne() and updateMany() usage
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding updateOne and updateMany is about intent and scope. updateOne modifies at most one document that matches your filter. It's appropriate when you expect a unique or single record, such as matching by _id or an email. updateMany applies the update to all documents matching the filter and is used for bulk adjustments like increasing stock across a category. The critical safety consideration is the filter: an empty filter object updates the entire collection. A common mistake is running updateMany with an unintended filter and changing thousands of documents. A simple safe workflow is to run the filter as a find query first to inspect the target set. Use projection or count to confirm results before applying updateMany. Examples in the lesson show incrementing stock for all documents in a category and changing a single user's email using updateOne. When using options like upsert, remember updateMany with upsert is rarely used in practice because inserting multiple documents requires different logic. Always verify changes with find() after the update. updateOne() and updateMany() usage means use updateone for targeted single-document changes and updatemany for controlled bulk updates; always preview your filter before executing.. In practical terms, choosing single-document updates versus bulk updates and using filters safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › updateOne & updateMany
updateOne()

Single-document updates

Use when updating a unique record. Confirm the filter targets one document.

Example
db.books.updateOne({ title: "The Great Novel" }, { $set: { price: 27.50, inStock: true } })
Run a find() first to inspect the matched document before updating.
updateMany()

Bulk updates

Use for applying the same update to many documents, but verify the filter carefully.

Example
db.books.updateMany({ genre: "Technology" }, { $inc: { stock: 10 } })
Double-check the filter—an empty filter would modify all documents.
Warning
Avoid updateMany({}) without a filter; preview with find() first.
Verify
Use count or projection to confirm the set of documents you will modify.
Key Takeaway
Pick the operation by scope and always preview targets first.

screens.title: Field operators: $set
screens.narratorSegment: The $set operator assigns a value to a field and adds the field if it does not exist. It is the most commonly used operator for partial updates. For example, you can update a user's email address and add a lastLogin timestamp in one call. $set does not remove other fields, which makes it safe for incremental changes. A common concrete use case is correcting a typo in a product title or adding a new metadata field; you do not want to accidentally delete arrays or details present in the document. One misconception is to think $set will merge nested objects deeply by default; when setting an embedded document path, you should use dot notation to target nested fields precisely. In the code example on screen, you will see how to set two fields in a single updateOne call and then verify the result with a find query. Key takeaway: use $set for controlled assignment and prefer dot notation to reach nested fields without replacing parent objects unintentionally. Field operators: $set means $set assigns or creates a field without affecting other fields; use dot notation for nested updates to avoid replacing parent objects.. In practical terms, set or add values safely without modifying other fields. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › $set
Definition

$set

Assigns a value to a field or adds it if missing without altering other fields.

Example update
db.users.updateOne(
  { username: "alice" },
  { $set: { email: "alice.s@example.com", lastLogin: new Date() } }
)
Verify with find(): db.users.find({ username: "alice" }).pretty()
Notes
  • Use dot notation to set nested fields: $set: { "profile.bio": "..." }.
  • $set does not deep-merge objects; setting a parent object replaces it.
  • Combine with $inc or $addToSet in the same update document when needed.
Key Takeaway
$set is the safe default for targeted assignments.

screens.title: Field operators: $inc, $unset, $rename
screens.narratorSegment: This screen covers three important field operators. $inc increments a numeric field by a given amount; it's atomic at the document level, making it safe for concurrent updates such as incrementing stock or login counters. If the field doesn't exist, $inc creates it with the increment value. $unset removes a field from a document; the value provided is ignored but required syntactically. Use $unset when a field is obsolete or you want to clear data. $rename changes a field name; it moves the value to a new key and removes the old one. Renaming is useful for schema migrations. Each operator has a concrete code example here and a verification step using find(). A common pitfall is assuming $inc will convert non-numeric values; it will error if the field exists with a non-numeric type. Also, $rename can overwrite an existing target field if names collide. Always preview documents and consider using a transaction for multi-step migrations. Practice these steps on a staging dataset before applying them to production. Field operators: $inc, $unset, $rename means $inc is atomic for numeric updates; $unset removes fields; $rename changes key names—always preview and verify to avoid collisions or type errors.. In practical terms, increment counters, remove fields, and rename keys safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › $inc, $unset, $rename
$inc
Atomic increments
db.products.updateOne({ name: "Laptop Pro X" }, { $inc: { stock: 5 } })
Creates stock if missing. Will error if stock exists as non-numeric type.
$unset
Remove a field
db.products.updateOne({ name: "Wireless Mouse" }, { $unset: { details: "" } })
Use to delete obsolete fields; value is ignored.
$rename
Rename a key
db.books.updateMany({}, { $rename: { publicationYear: "yearPublished" } })
Be careful: target name may overwrite existing fields.
Misconception
$inc will not convert strings to numbers; ensure the existing type is numeric.
Caution
$rename may collide with existing fields; preview before renaming across many documents.
Key Takeaway
Use these operators for specific field-level changes and verify types and collisions first.

screens.title: $push and $each
screens.narratorSegment: $push adds an element to an array field, and if the field does not exist it creates an array with the new element. When you need to add multiple elements at once, combine $push with $each to supply an array of values. Use $push with caution when order matters or when documents have large arrays, as frequent growth of large arrays may impact performance. A concrete example is adding tags to a product: pushing a single tag appends it to the tags array, while $each appends an ordered set of values in one atomic update. A common misconception is to expect $push to prevent duplicates; it does not. If you need to avoid duplicate entries, use $addToSet instead. Practice a before/after check for array operations to verify the expected order and elements were added. Consider array-sizing limits and whether a different modeling pattern (separate collection) suits very large arrays. $push and $each means $push appends elements and $each adds multiple elements in one update; it does not prevent duplicates—use $addtoset for deduplication.. In practical terms, add single or multiple elements to arrays and shape how items are appended. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › $push & $each
Single push
Add one element
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Laptop Pro X" },
  { $push: { tags: "new-arrival" } }
)
If tags did not exist, tags becomes ["new-arrival"].
Multiple elements
Use $each to add many items atomically
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Laptop Pro X" },
  { $push: { tags: { $each: ["popular", "high-demand"] } } }
)
Maintains order of appended elements in one update.
Performance
Frequent growth of large arrays can impact performance; consider a separate collection for very large lists.
Misconception
$push does not deduplicate; duplicates are allowed unless using $addToSet.
Key Takeaway
Use $push for appending and $each for multiple elements; switch to $addToSet if duplicates are a concern.

screens.title: $addToSet and $pop
screens.narratorSegment: $addToSet is the safe choice when you want to add an element only if it does not already exist in the array. It prevents duplicates and is especially useful for tag lists or membership arrays. For example, adding a 'gaming' tag to a product will succeed only if that tag isn't present, avoiding repeated entries. $pop removes elements from an array by position: passing -1 removes the first element and 1 removes the last element. Use $pop when you need to trim the front or end of an array, for instance pruning a recent-activity list. A common pitfall is expecting $addToSet to behave like a set for embedded documents with different shapes—uniqueness is based on the equality of the stored values. When working with complex embedded documents, consider a targeted $pull to remove specific entries or a normalized design. Practice verifying array content after each operation with a find() query to confirm the intended modification. Final takeaway: choose $addToSet for deduplication and $pop for positional removal, and inspect array shapes when working with embedded documents. $addToSet and $pop means $addtoset prevents duplicates; $pop removes first or last items. verify array shapes and duplicates when using these operators.. In practical terms, prevent duplicates and remove first or last elements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

$addToSet
Add only if not present
db.products.updateOne(

Remove by position

Definition

$pull

Removes all array elements that match a value or a query condition.

Remove by value

screens.title: Using upsert: create or update
screens.narratorSegment: Upsert is an option you pass with updateOne or updateMany that tells MongoDB to insert a new document if no existing document matches the filter. This is handy for create-or-update workflows like syncing a user profile: if a user record exists, update it; otherwise create it. The example demonstrates using upsert:true to set fields for a new book if it doesn't already exist. Upsert will merge the update document into the inserted document, so include required fields in the $set. A misconception is to expect upsert to behave differently across updateMany; upsert with updateMany is unusual because inserting many new documents from a single filter is not possible—the server inserts a single new document when no match is found. After an upsert, verify insertion with a find query to ensure the expected fields were set. Also consider whether unique indexes or validation rules will reject the inserted document. Use upsert when a single create-or-update is appropriate and always inspect the resulting document. Using upsert: create or update means upsert:true inserts a new document if no match is found; structure your update so inserted documents contain required fields and verify after the operation.. Example

  { title: "New Release", author: "Author X" },
  { $set: { price: 30.00, inStock: true, genre: "Fantasy", publicationYear: 2024 } },

screens.title: Atomicity, performance, and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: MongoDB ensures atomicity at the document level: a single-document update operation completes entirely or not at all, which keeps the document consistent even under concurrent modifications. This makes operators like $inc safe for incrementing counters without race conditions on the document. However, atomicity does not extend across multiple documents unless you use multi-document transactions. Performance considerations include the cost of frequent updates to very large documents or arrays; updating large embedded arrays often triggers more input and output. A common pitfall is using replaceOne inadvertently and removing fields, or using updateMany with too-broad a filter. Another safety rule is to preview your filter with a find and consider backup or staging for large migrations. Use indexes to make filters efficient and think about modeling alternatives—if an array grows unbounded, a separate collection for items may be a better choice. When migrations require many structural changes, consider breaking work into smaller steps and using transactions where cross-document consistency is required. Atomicity, performance, and common pitfalls means updates are atomic per document; watch performance on large documents and avoid broad filters or unintended replaceone calls.. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Atomicity & Safety

Atomicity and common pitfalls

Single-document updates are atomic, but multi-document consistency requires transactions. Plan updates to avoid data loss and performance problems.

Pitfall: replaceOne misuse
Replacing when you meant to modify will drop fields. Confirm the replacement document includes everything you need.
Pitfall: broad updateMany
An empty filter updates all documents. Preview with find() before running the update.
Performance
Frequent updates of large arrays or documents increase I/O. Consider schema changes or separate collections for many child items.
Atomic operations
Operators like $inc are atomic on a document, so they are safe for concurrent increments.
Pro tip
Always run your filter as a find() and confirm counts before updating large sets.
Key Takeaway
Document-level atomicity preserves individual changes, but safe updates need preview and careful modeling decisions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Bookstore Activity

Step-by-step starter template

Use the starter code below in mongosh. Inspect, update, and verify each step.

use bookstoreDB

// 1. Update a single book's price and inStock status
db.books.updateOne(
  { title: "The Great Novel" },
  { $set: { price: 27.50, inStock: true } }
)

// 2. Increment stock for all "Technology" books
db.books.updateMany(
  { genre: "Technology" },
  { $inc: { stock: 10 } }
)

// 3. Add a new tag using $addToSet
db.books.updateOne(
  { title: "The Great Novel" },
  { $addToSet: { tags: "award-winning" } }
)

// 4. Remove a tag from a book
db.books.updateOne(
  { title: "Data Science Handbook" },
  { $pull: { tags: "programming" } }
)

// 5. Upsert a new book
db.books.updateOne(
  { title: "New Release", author: "Author X" },
  { $set: { price: 30.00, inStock: true, genre: "Fantasy", publicationYear: 2024 } },
  { upsert: true }
)

// Verify updates
db.books.find({ title: "The Great Novel" }).pretty()
db.books.find({ genre: "Technology" }).pretty()
db.books.find({ title: "New Release" }).pretty()
Verification
Always run find() queries after updates to confirm expected changes.
Staging
Practice on staging data before running updates on production collections.
Safety
Preview filters with find() and check counts to avoid unintended updates.

Second, updateOne and updateMany paired with operators like $set, $inc, $unset, and $rename let you change specific fields safely—prefer these for incremental updates. Third, array operators ($push, $each, $addToSet, $pop, $pull) are powerful for managing lists but require attention: $addToSet prevents duplicates, $push allows duplicates and ordering, $pull removes matching elements, and $pop removes by position. Always preview filters with find(), verify results after updating, and be mindful that atomicity applies at the document level. These three concepts will help you design safe update operations and reduce the risk of data loss or unintended modifications in production. fullNarratorScript:
This lesson will give you a clear, practical view of how MongoDB lets you change data. You will learn the difference between replacing an entire document and updating only specific fields, and why partial updates are usually safer and faster. We'll introduce updateOne and updateMany for targeted changes, explain important field operators like $set, $inc, $unset, and $rename, and then step through array-focused operators such as $push, $addToSet, $pop, and $pull for adding, deduplicating, and removing elements. You will also see the upsert option, which can create-or-update a document in a single call, and we will highlight common mistakes like accidentally running updateMany with an empty filter. Throughout the lesson, we frame each operator with short code examples and before/after states so you can see the transformation. By the end you will know when to use replaceOne versus updateOne, how to manipulate numeric and array fields atomically, and how to design safe updates that minimize data loss and performance issues. Ready to explore the operators and practice a bookstore inventory scenario to make this concrete?

In this chapter you will build four practical skills that make document updates reliable and efficient. First, you will clearly understand the difference between replacing a whole document and updating individual fields, and why partial updates often prevent accidental data loss. For example, replacing a document will remove fields you did not include, which can be surprising if you expect a small change. Second, you will learn to use updateOne and updateMany correctly, choosing the right method when you need to change a single record versus many records at once and avoiding broad filters that update the entire collection. Third, you will practice field operators such as $set and $inc to change or increment values atomically, and $unset or $rename to remove or rename fields. These operators let you evolve documents without replacing them. Fourth, you will master array update operators—$push, $addToSet, $pop, and $pull—to add, deduplicate, and remove array elements safely. Each objective will include a short example and a verification step so you can check results in mongosh.

These objectives focus on practice and safety you'll need as a developer. You will be able to perform create-or-update flows using the upsert option, which inserts when no match exists and updates when one does. We will show a concrete upsert example and discuss when it's appropriate. You will also learn to avoid common mistakes such as using replaceOne when you intended a partial change, or running updateMany with an empty filter and unintentionally modifying every document. Another objective is to verify updates using queries and the. pretty() output so you can confirm before moving on. Finally, you will learn to reason about atomicity: updates are atomic at the document level in MongoDB, so single-document operators like $inc are safe for concurrent increments, but multi-document consistency requires transactions. Each objective includes a short verification step or rule of thumb to keep updates safe in production.

Let's compare replacing a document with replaceOne and applying targeted changes with updateOne. replaceOne takes a matching filter and substitutes a new document for the matched one. That means every field not present in the replacement will be removed, except for _id which is preserved. This makes replaceOne appropriate when you intentionally want a complete structural change or to reset a document. In contrast, updateOne with operators modifies only specified fields; it leaves all other fields untouched. A typical pattern uses $set with updateOne to change some fields safely. For example, if a product document has fields stock, tags, and details, replacing it without including tags will remove that information. A common misconception is to assume replaceOne behaves like a partial update; it does not. Always inspect the replacement body. In practice, prefer updateOne with $set for incremental changes, and reserve replaceOne for structural rewrites or migrations. To check your work, run a find query before and after and compare fields. Which approach fits your maintenance policy and rollback plan? replaceOne() versus updateOne() means use replaceone only when you intend a full overwrite; use updateone with $set to change fields without losing other data.. In practical terms, when overwriting a document deletes fields versus when to update only what you need. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding updateOne and updateMany is about intent and scope. updateOne modifies at most one document that matches your filter. It's appropriate when you expect a unique or single record, such as matching by _id or an email. updateMany applies the update to all documents matching the filter and is used for bulk adjustments like increasing stock across a category. The critical safety consideration is the filter: an empty filter object updates the entire collection. A common mistake is running updateMany with an unintended filter and changing thousands of documents. A simple safe workflow is to run the filter as a find query first to inspect the target set. Use projection or count to confirm results before applying updateMany. Examples in the lesson show incrementing stock for all documents in a category and changing a single user's email using updateOne. When using options like upsert, remember updateMany with upsert is rarely used in practice because inserting multiple documents requires different logic. Always verify changes with find() after the update. updateOne() and updateMany() usage means use updateone for targeted single-document changes and updatemany for controlled bulk updates; always preview your filter before executing.. In practical terms, choosing single-document updates versus bulk updates and using filters safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The $set operator assigns a value to a field and adds the field if it does not exist. It is the most commonly used operator for partial updates. For example, you can update a user's email address and add a lastLogin timestamp in one call. $set does not remove other fields, which makes it safe for incremental changes. A common concrete use case is correcting a typo in a product title or adding a new metadata field; you do not want to accidentally delete arrays or details present in the document. One misconception is to think $set will merge nested objects deeply by default; when setting an embedded document path, you should use dot notation to target nested fields precisely. In the code example on screen, you will see how to set two fields in a single updateOne call and then verify the result with a find query. Key takeaway: use $set for controlled assignment and prefer dot notation to reach nested fields without replacing parent objects unintentionally. Field operators: $set means $set assigns or creates a field without affecting other fields; use dot notation for nested updates to avoid replacing parent objects.. In practical terms, set or add values safely without modifying other fields. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This screen covers three important field operators. $inc increments a numeric field by a given amount; it's atomic at the document level, making it safe for concurrent updates such as incrementing stock or login counters. If the field doesn't exist, $inc creates it with the increment value. $unset removes a field from a document; the value provided is ignored but required syntactically. Use $unset when a field is obsolete or you want to clear data. $rename changes a field name; it moves the value to a new key and removes the old one. Renaming is useful for schema migrations. Each operator has a concrete code example here and a verification step using find(). A common pitfall is assuming $inc will convert non-numeric values; it will error if the field exists with a non-numeric type. Also, $rename can overwrite an existing target field if names collide. Always preview documents and consider using a transaction for multi-step migrations. Practice these steps on a staging dataset before applying them to production. Field operators: $inc, $unset, $rename means $inc is atomic for numeric updates; $unset removes fields; $rename changes key names—always preview and verify to avoid collisions or type errors.. In practical terms, increment counters, remove fields, and rename keys safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

$push adds an element to an array field, and if the field does not exist it creates an array with the new element. When you need to add multiple elements at once, combine $push with $each to supply an array of values. Use $push with caution when order matters or when documents have large arrays, as frequent growth of large arrays may impact performance. A concrete example is adding tags to a product: pushing a single tag appends it to the tags array, while $each appends an ordered set of values in one atomic update. A common misconception is to expect $push to prevent duplicates; it does not. If you need to avoid duplicate entries, use $addToSet instead. Practice a before/after check for array operations to verify the expected order and elements were added. Consider array-sizing limits and whether a different modeling pattern (separate collection) suits very large arrays. $push and $each means $push appends elements and $each adds multiple elements in one update; it does not prevent duplicates—use $addtoset for deduplication.. In practical terms, add single or multiple elements to arrays and shape how items are appended. To wrap up, remember three essential ideas. First, replaceOne overwrites the entire document except for _id; use it only when you intend a full replacement. Second, updateOne and updateMany paired with operators like $set, $inc, $unset, and $rename let you change specific fields safely—prefer these for incremental updates. Third, array operators ($push, $each, $addToSet, $pop, $pull) are powerful for managing lists but require attention: $addToSet prevents duplicates, $push allows duplicates and ordering, $pull removes matching elements, and $pop removes by position.
